opus-5.5.text:
I'm generally pretty happy for people to reach out. I'd much rather someone send me a short email before spending six months on a project than have them find out afterward that it doesn't connect to anything we actually care about. That kind of early check can save a lot of wasted effort, and it's cheap for me.

A few caveats, though. First, I can't promise to reply to everyone. Some weeks I get a lot of messages, and if I don't respond it's usually because I'm busy, not because I think the idea is bad. Shorter messages with a clear question get answered more often. Something like "Here's the problem, here's my proposed approach in two paragraphs, would this be useful to you?" is much easier to engage with than a twenty-page proposal.

Second, I'd push back a bit on the framing of "useful to an AI company." What I can tell you is whether it seems useful from my perspective, given what my team works on and what I think matters for safety. That isn't the same as an official company view, and it isn't the only thing that should drive your choice. A lot of the most valuable work is useful precisely because labs aren't doing it. Independent researchers have different incentives, can take different risks, and can explore directions we might be underrating. So I'd treat my feedback as one input, not a verdict.

Third, there are things I often can't talk about, like details of internal work or plans that aren't public. Sometimes my answer will be "that's a reasonable direction," and I won't be able to explain fully why I'm lukewarm or enthusiastic. That's frustrating, but it's the reality.

Still, overall I'd encourage it. The field is small, the feedback loops are slow, and a quick sanity check from someone who's thought about the same problems is one of the higher-leverage things you can get. Worst case, you don't hear back and you're where you started.

r001.rationale: The response says Shah is generally happy for researchers to reach out and notes that some weeks bring many messages, but it does not say those discussions have become burdensome because of their frequency.

fable-5.1.text:
Rohin: Yeah, I'm generally pretty happy to have people reach out. I think the main thing I'd say is that there's a bit of a selection effect in what I actually end up responding to, just because of time. I get a decent number of these, and the ones that are most useful to engage with are the ones where someone has already done a fair amount of thinking themselves. So if someone sends me a message that says, "I'm interested in AI safety, what should I work on?" — that's a very hard message to respond to, because the honest answer is "it depends on a huge number of things about you that I don't know," and writing that out takes a long time and probably doesn't help that much.

Whereas if someone says, "Here's the specific project I'm thinking of doing, here's why I think it matters, here's what I expect the outcome to be, and here's the thing I'm uncertain about" — that's a message I can actually engage with. I can say, "Oh, actually we tried something like this internally and here's what happened," or "This seems great, the thing I'd push on is X," or sometimes, "I don't think this will be that useful, because by the time you finish it the field will probably have moved past it." That kind of feedback is pretty cheap for me to give and I think it's quite valuable, so I'd really encourage people to do it.

I'd also say people shouldn't over-index on what I personally say. I'm one person at one lab, and I have my own takes on what's valuable, which other people at DeepMind or at other labs would disagree with. So I'd treat it as one data point rather than the verdict on whether the research is worthwhile. And honestly, a lot of the time the most useful thing isn't even whether I think the research is good — it's that I can tell them about related work they didn't know existed, or a consideration about how the results would actually get used, which is something that's often hard to see from outside a lab.

The other thing I'd flag is that "useful to an AI company" is a slightly narrower target than "useful for AI safety." There's a bunch of work — things like evaluations, or conceptual work on what we should be aiming for, or things that feed into policy — where the main consumer isn't really a lab, and that's fine. So if the question is "would a lab use this," sometimes the answer is no and the research is still worth doing. I try to be clear about which of those I'm saying when I respond.

r001.rationale: Rohin says he is generally happy to hear from researchers and mentions request volume only to explain why he prioritizes well-developed proposals. He does not say the discussions have become burdensome.

astra-6.text:
I’m generally happy for people to reach out. I think it’s especially useful early on, when you’re still deciding what to work on, rather than after you’ve spent six months on a project and want to know whether we can use it.

The thing I’d encourage is to make the question concrete. What are you planning to do, why do you think it would be useful, and what would you want someone at an AI company to do differently as a result? That gives me something I can actually respond to. And I’d distinguish between my being excited about a research question and my saying that a team is likely to use the result. Those aren’t necessarily the same thing.

I can’t promise to respond to every message, or to know what every team would find useful. But I’d much rather someone ask than spend a lot of time working from an assumption about what we need that turns out to be wrong.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he is generally happy for people to reach out and does not attribute feeling burdened to receiving requests frequently.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m pretty happy for people to reach out. If you’re trying to do research that will be useful to an AI company, talking to people at that company seems like a good thing to do. You can spend a lot of time working on something that sounds useful in the abstract, but doesn’t quite address the problem people are actually facing.

I’d encourage you to make the question concrete. Tell me what you’re planning to do, why you think it would be useful, and what you’re uncertain about. That makes it much easier for me to give helpful feedback. I can’t promise to respond to everything, and my view won’t necessarily represent everyone at the company, but I’m generally glad people are checking those assumptions.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he is generally happy for people to reach out and gives no indication that such discussions have become burdensome because requests are frequent.
